summary: A proposal by John Day for a File Access Protocol, an extension of FTP that lets a program work with remote files more like a local file system. Day offers it as a starting point and asks for comments, including on holey Tenex files and record-oriented systems.

plainLanguage.summary: A plan to let programs use files on faraway computers as if they were on their own, not only copy them.

questions: what is the file access protocol
what is a file pointer in ftp
subtitle: A proposed extension to FTP that reads and writes parts of remote files instead of whole ones.

tldr.problem: FTP moves whole files, so a program that needs only part of a remote file must transfer and store all of it.
tldr.mechanism: The File Access Protocol (FAP) adds a file pointer and six commands to FTP: OPEN, CLOS, SETP, GETP, READ and WRIT, so a process can say where to start and how much to move.
tldr.outcome: It is a proposal offered as a jumping-off point. John Day says he would eventually like FAP merged with FTP into a richer whole.

today: The unit metadata lists this RFC's status as Unknown and records no replacement. It is a proposal for comment.

sections.title: Purpose and Reuse of FTP
sections.content:
The File Access Protocol (FAP) lets processes access non-local files sequentially or non-sequentially. It is an extension of FTP, not a subsystem like the proposed Mail Protocol. Only the part of a file a process needs is transferred, which holds down transmission time and storage. The rationale is the same as for "random-accessed" files in an operating system.

FAP uses FTP's connection model, data representations, and transmission methods. In Stream mode the minimum byte size rises to 4 bits and a new control code (value 4) marks "end of transmission", so the connection need not be closed after each access. In Block mode, bit 5 of the header's descriptor field marks the end of transmission.
sections.plainLanguage: FAP builds on FTP, the existing way to copy files, and adds a way to ask for only the piece you need.

sections.title: Implementation Rules
sections.content: The RFC says no host should have to give network users a service it does not give its local users. Some systems allow random access to some files only, cannot move the byte pointer backwards without closing and reopening, or cannot mix reading and writing. The rules are: allow an access if the system normally allows it for that file; do not simulate a facility if the simulation has side effects; and publish your implementation's capabilities in NIC documents.
sections.plainLanguage: A computer should not have to do tricks for visitors that it does not do for its own users.

sections.title: The File Pointer and Commands
sections.content:
Any implementation needs the file pointer and all six commands. The pointer counts logical bytes and can be B (beginning, byte 0), E (end, byte n for an n byte file), or any number between. OPEN takes a direction (R, W or B for both) and a pathname, and leaves the pointer at B. SETP moves the pointer and GETP reports it. READ and WRIT take a byte count or ALL and update the pointer. CLOS closes the open file, and closing with no file open is not an error.

Replies reuse FTP codes and add new ones, such as 480 for EOR, 481 for EOF, 482 for file not open, 483 for the pointer value, and 402 when a command is not implemented for the requested value.
sections.plainLanguage: The bookmark can go to the start, the end, or any spot between. You then say "read this much" or "write this much" from the bookmark.

sections.title: Open Questions in the Cover Note
sections.content: Day asks for comments from the TENEX crowd on "holey" files, and suggests record-oriented systems may need an extra command or parameter. The sequence OPEN R FOO.BAR, READ ALL, CLOS is equivalent to RETR FOO.BAR. He notes that three-digit reply codes are not enough and suggests a five-digit interim scheme.
sections.plainLanguage: The author admits he is unsure about a few odd cases and asks others to help.

items.label: Open file
items.desc: Opens a file for read (R), write (W) or both (B); the pointer starts at B.

items.label: Close file
items.desc: Closes the open file, if any.

items.label: Set pointer
items.desc: Sets the file pointer to B, E or a decimal number.

items.label: Get pointer
items.desc: Returns the file pointer as a decimal number.

items.label: Read bytes
items.desc: Moves the given number of bytes, or ALL, from server to user.

items.label: Write bytes
items.desc: Accepts the given number of bytes, or ALL, from user to server.
